Why I’m studying kinesiology

Matthew Ehsan · Student founder · Texas Tech University

I’m studying kinesiology at Texas Tech University with the goal of attending medical school. My interest in sports medicine and physical medicine and rehabilitation grew from playing sports and going through rehabilitation myself.

I started with basketball, then moved into track and field, where I broke a few records. I later took up powerlifting and broke records at McKinney High School. After two years of strength training, my parents agreed to let me play football. I joined the varsity team, played several positions, and became one of its captains. I enjoyed being part of the team.

A shoulder injury introduced me to rehabilitation. I did not have shoulder surgery. Learning to perform exercises correctly and rebuild strength helped me understand the importance of technique and a structured recovery plan. That experience made me want to learn more about how the body moves, how injuries happen, and how rehabilitation helps people regain function.

I also sustained a serious pinky injury and continue to live with its effects. Surgery will be required. I enjoy playing piano as well as sports.

My two cousins, Sam Ehsan, MD, and Pasha Ehsan, MD, specialize in orthopedic surgery and physical medicine and rehabilitation, respectively.

I started this student athlete education initiative to make information about injury prevention and recovery easier to find and understand. I want students to know what questions to ask and when to seek professional help. My role is to learn and organize educational resources, not to diagnose injuries or give treatment advice.

For now, my focus is on completing my kinesiology degree and preparing for medical school. I’m interested in becoming a physician who helps people understand their injuries, consider their treatment options, and work toward recovery.

Clinical support and educational scope

The intended educational areas span medicine, orthopedics, physical medicine and rehabilitation, psychology, and marriage and family therapy. Professional review will be credited only when completed by the named reviewer.

This independent initiative does not represent any university, employer, sports team, or medical institution.

Stop play and call 911 for an emergency. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, suspected neck or spine injury, seizure, severe heat illness, new weakness or numbness, or worsening neurologic symptoms after a head impact require urgent action. A suspected concussion means no same day return to play.

The order below is a practical U.S. priority ranking based on broad youth and school participation, visibility, and injury education needs. It is not a claim that one sport is universally more popular than another.

Body and mind belong together

Our educational mission includes performance pressure, confidence, injury recovery, burnout, body image, team relationships, and transitions beyond competitive sports.

An athlete’s worth extends beyond a roster spot, scholarship, draft selection, or professional contract. Seeking support deserves the same respect as training and recovery.

A coach’s preparation checklist

  • Know the team’s emergency action plan and who activates it.
  • Identify the athletic trainer and local medical support.
  • Make room for athletes to report concerns privately.
  • Use the sport guides to prepare questions for qualified professionals.
  • Keep educational guidance separate from diagnosis and clearance decisions.

1Basketball

Most common: ankle sprain, ACL and meniscus injury, patellar tendinopathy, finger injury, muscle strain, and concussion.

Prevent: neuromuscular warmups, landing and cutting technique, progressive workload, hip and leg strength, well fitted shoes, sleep, hydration, and recovery days.

Warning signs: a pop with rapid swelling, knee giving way, inability to bear weight, visible deformity, joint locking, or headache, confusion, vomiting, and balance trouble after contact.

Early care and return: stop play, protect the area, use relative rest and cold for comfort, and obtain prompt evaluation when function is impaired. Rehabilitation should restore motion, strength, balance, jumping, cutting, and confidence before clearance.

2American football

Most common: concussion, shoulder instability, ACL and MCL injury, ankle sprain, hamstring strain, hand injury, and heat illness.

Prevent: proper tackling, neck and trunk strength, progressive contact, fitted equipment, hydration, heat acclimatization, and immediate symptom reporting.

Warning signs: severe neck pain, weakness, collapse, confusion, repeated vomiting, breathing difficulty, or a deformed joint.

Early care and return: remove from play. Do not move an athlete with a suspected spine injury. Activate emergency care for red flags and use diagnosis specific rehabilitation before graded return.

3Track and field

Most common: hamstring strain, shin pain, bone stress injury, Achilles or patellar tendinopathy, ankle sprain, and low back pain.

Prevent: gradual mileage and sprint progression, event specific technique, strength training, adequate calories and iron, appropriate footwear, and planned recovery.

Warning signs: focal bone pain, night pain, limping, persistent swelling, or declining performance with unusual fatigue.

Early care and return: stop impact loading for suspected bone stress injury and seek assessment. Return requires pain free daily activity, restored strength, and gradual running progression.

4Soccer

Most common: ankle sprain, ACL injury, hamstring and groin strain, knee contusion, concussion, and overuse pain.

Prevent: structured neuromuscular warmups, landing and cutting practice, hip and hamstring strength, workload control, and safe play.

Warning signs: knee instability or rapid swelling, inability to run, significant groin pain, or any concussion symptom.

Early care and return: remove from play and assess. Rehabilitation must rebuild running, direction change, kicking, and contact tolerance before clearance.

5Baseball

Most common: shoulder and elbow overuse, UCL injury, rotator cuff irritation, hamstring strain, ankle sprain, and hand trauma.

Prevent: pitch count and rest rules, seasonal breaks from throwing, whole body strength, sound mechanics, and early reporting of pain or velocity loss.

Warning signs: medial elbow pain, shoulder weakness, numbness, loss of control, a pop, or altered throwing mechanics.

Early care and return: stop painful throwing, obtain assessment, and use a criteria based interval throwing program rather than returning by date alone.

6Volleyball

Most common: ankle sprain, jumper’s knee, shoulder overuse, finger injury, and low back pain.

Prevent: landing mechanics, ankle balance work, shoulder and scapular strength, jump count management, and recovery.

Warning signs: inability to bear weight, recurrent instability, loss of shoulder strength, or persistent focal back pain.

Early care and return: protect the injury, restore motion and strength, then progress jumping, landing, serving, and hitting.

7Softball

Most common: shoulder overuse, elbow pain, ACL injury, ankle sprain, hand trauma, and hamstring strain.

Prevent: monitor pitching workload, strengthen the kinetic chain, practice cutting and landing, rotate positions when appropriate, and schedule recovery.

Warning signs: progressive pitching pain, weakness, swelling, instability, or altered mechanics.

Early care and return: stop painful pitching or play, assess early, and complete a graduated throwing, fielding, running, and hitting progression.

8Wrestling

Most common: shoulder and knee sprain, concussion, neck strain, skin infection, and dehydration related illness.

Prevent: safe technique, mat hygiene and skin checks, neck and shoulder strength, hydration, and no rapid weight cutting.

Warning signs: weakness or numbness, severe neck pain, confusion, spreading skin lesions, fever, or collapse.

Early care and return: stop competition, protect a possible spine injury, cover and assess skin lesions, and return only after condition specific clearance.

9Swimming and diving

Most common: swimmer’s shoulder, low back pain, knee pain, ear problems, and diving related head or neck trauma.

Prevent: stroke technique, balanced shoulder strength, gradual yardage, mobility, dry land conditioning, and supervised diving progression.

Warning signs: neurologic symptoms after diving, persistent weakness, night pain, or pain that alters the stroke.

Early care and return: stop painful strokes or diving, urgently protect suspected neck injuries, and rebuild volume and technique gradually.

10Tennis

Most common: ankle sprain, lateral elbow tendinopathy, shoulder pain, wrist injury, and low back strain.

Prevent: progressive court time, racquet and grip fit, trunk and shoulder strength, footwork practice, and recovery between tournaments.

Warning signs: loss of grip strength, persistent swelling, instability, or pain that changes the serve.

Early care and return: reduce provoking load, assess technique and equipment, restore capacity, then progress groundstrokes, serves, and match play.

11Cross country

Most common: bone stress injury, shin pain, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar pain, knee pain, and relative energy deficiency.

Prevent: gradual mileage, varied surfaces, strength training, adequate nutrition, sleep, and early response to focal pain.

Warning signs: localized bone tenderness, limping, pain at rest, recurrent injury, fatigue, or menstrual disruption.

Early care and return: stop running when stress injury is suspected, seek evaluation, and use a walk run progression after healing criteria are met.

12Gymnastics

Most common: wrist stress injury, ankle sprain, ACL injury, low back stress injury, shoulder instability, and concussion.

Prevent: supervised skill progression, landing mechanics, equipment checks, workload limits, strength, nutrition, and recovery.

Warning signs: focal back or wrist pain, neurologic symptoms, joint instability, or pain during ordinary activity.

Early care and return: stop the painful skill, assess promptly, and return from basics to full routines only after strength and impact tolerance recover.

13Cheerleading

Most common: concussion, ankle and wrist sprain, shoulder instability, knee injury, and serious fall related injury.

Prevent: qualified supervision, progressive stunt training, trained spotters, appropriate surfaces, strength, and concussion recognition.

Warning signs: neck or back pain after a fall, weakness, numbness, confusion, vomiting, severe headache, or loss of consciousness.

Early care and return: stabilize and activate emergency care for spine or neurologic red flags. Return should be staged and medically cleared.

14Lacrosse

Most common: ankle and knee sprain, concussion, shoulder injury, hand trauma, and muscle strain.

Prevent: fitted equipment, safe checking technique, neck and shoulder strength, neuromuscular warmups, and workload progression.

Warning signs: neurologic symptoms, rapid swelling, instability, deformity, or inability to bear weight.

Early care and return: remove from play, assess concussion separately, protect joints, and restore sprinting, cutting, stick work, and contact tolerance.

15Ice hockey

Most common: concussion, shoulder separation, knee ligament injury, groin strain, laceration, and hand injury.

Prevent: fitted equipment, safe checking, neck and shoulder conditioning, skate control, blade safety, and immediate symptom reporting.

Warning signs: confusion, neck pain, weakness, uncontrolled bleeding, joint deformity, or inability to skate or bear weight.

Early care and return: remove from ice, control bleeding, protect the neck when indicated, and use a progressive skating and contact plan.

16Golf

Most common: low back pain, golfer’s elbow, wrist and shoulder overuse, and heat illness.

Prevent: swing coaching, trunk and hip strength, gradual range volume, warmup, hydration, sun protection, and safe equipment carrying.

Warning signs: radiating pain, weakness, numbness, severe night pain, or heat related confusion.

Early care and return: reduce painful volume, assess neurologic or persistent focal symptoms, and rebuild swing repetitions gradually.

17Powerlifting and weight training

Most common: low back strain, shoulder and elbow overuse, knee pain, muscle tear, and hand injury.

Prevent: sound technique, trained spotting, progressive loading, fatigue management, full recovery, appropriate equipment, and no ego driven attempts.

Warning signs: a pop with weakness or bruising, radiating pain, numbness, loss of bowel or bladder control, chest pain, or fainting.

Early care and return: stop the lift, seek urgent care for neurologic or systemic red flags, and rebuild movement quality and submaximal load before heavy attempts.

18Martial arts and boxing

Most common: concussion, facial injury, hand and wrist injury, shoulder instability, knee sprain, and dehydration.

Prevent: qualified coaching, controlled sparring exposure, fitted equipment, hand wrapping, neck strength, hydration, and no training through concussion symptoms.

Warning signs: repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, unequal pupils, weakness, seizure, loss of consciousness, or vision change.

Early care and return: stop contact immediately and obtain emergency assessment for neurologic red flags. Return to contact must follow a medical protocol.

19Cycling

Most common: concussion, fracture, road rash, knee pain, neck and back pain, and hand numbness.

Prevent: helmet use, visible clothing, bike fit, road awareness, progressive mileage, strength, and fueling.

Warning signs: neurologic symptoms after a crash, severe chest or abdominal pain, deformity, uncontrolled bleeding, or persistent numbness.

Early care and return: ensure scene safety, call emergency services for major trauma, clean superficial wounds appropriately, and obtain evaluation before riding again.

20Pickleball

Most common: ankle sprain, Achilles rupture, knee strain, shoulder pain, and falls.

Prevent: dynamic warmup, calf and leg strength, court shoes, progressive play time, balance training, hydration, and adequate space.

Warning signs: a sudden snap behind the ankle, inability to push off, marked swelling, deformity, head injury symptoms, or inability to bear weight.

Early care and return: stop play, protect the area, assess a suspected Achilles rupture promptly, and progress court movement only after function returns.

Sources and further reading

For suspected concussion, remove the athlete from play immediately. No return on the day of injury, and no return until cleared by a healthcare provider.

Diagnosis, imaging, treatment, rehabilitation, and return to play must be individualized by qualified professionals. Athletes should follow their clinician, athletic trainer, school, league, and governing body requirements.
